1.text:
Where Does Indiana's Weather Come From?

In Deck 11 we built the atmosphere and learned how the greenhouse effect works. Now we're going to set that air and the oceans in motion. Where does the rain on your school come from? Why does Indiana get tornadoes? And what's the difference between a cold week and a changing climate?

We'll go in three parts. First, the water cycle and where Earth's water is stored. Second, how sunlight and Earth's spin drive the seasons, winds and ocean currents. Third, weather and climate: fronts, storms, ice ages and the records that show our climate changing.

As always, we'll visit other worlds. Venus lost its oceans, Mars has seasons with frozen CO2, and Titan rains methane instead of water.

Did you know? Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, in the middle of our winter.

2.text:
Today I Can...

Here's what you'll be able to do by the end of this deck. Copy these into your notebook as "I can" statements and rate yourself 1 to 3 on each one.

I can trace water through the cycle and read the water budget. I can present the water cycle locally and globally, with human effects. I can explain uneven heating and the seasons from the 23.4° tilt. I can model how the Coriolis effect bends winds into three cells. I can explain gyres, El Niño and La Niña, and how far their effects reach. I can model the thermohaline conveyor using heat, salt and density.

I can chart humidity, pressure and temperature, and explain fronts. I can explain Indiana severe weather and write a storm plan. I can tell weather from climate and explain Milankovitch cycles. I can read the CO2 and temperature records and their causes. And, as an enrichment goal, I can compare water and seasons on Venus and Mars.

3.text:
Water Is Always on the Move

The water cycle is the nonstop movement of water between ocean, air, land, ice and life. The Sun powers it. Sunlight drives evaporation, turning liquid water from the ocean into invisible vapor. Plants add vapor too, by transpiration: they pull water from the soil and release it from their leaves.

High up, the vapor cools and condenses into clouds made of tiny droplets or ice crystals. Then gravity takes over. Precipitation falls as rain or snow. Some water becomes runoff, flowing downhill into streams and lakes. Some soaks in by infiltration and becomes groundwater, which flows slowly through soil and rock back to streams and the ocean. And some gets stored for a long time as snow and ice.

A single water molecule can take lots of different paths. It might spend a few days in the air, or thousands of years in a glacier.

Did you know? Titan, Saturn's largest moon, has its own cycle with clouds, rain, rivers and lakes. But they're made of liquid methane and ethane, not water.

4.text:
Where Earth's Water Is

96.5% of Earth's water is in the oceans, and about 71% of the surface is water. So there's plenty of water, right? Sort of. Only 2.5% of all water is fresh.

Now zoom in on that fresh water. Ice and snow lock up 68.7% of it. Groundwater holds 30.1%. That leaves just 1.2% as surface and other fresh water, which includes ground ice, soil moisture, the air, swamps and living things. Zoom in once more: lakes hold 20.9% of that small slice, and rivers just 0.49%.

That's worth a second look, because rivers and lakes supply most of the water people use every day. A tiny share of Earth's water does a huge amount of work.

Did you know? During the last ice age, so much water was frozen into ice sheets that sea level was about 122 m lower than today.

5.text:
Why Water Is Special

Water has two strange properties that shape our weather and keep lakes alive. The first is its high specific heat: the energy it takes to warm 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C. Water needs 4,184 J to warm 1 kg by 1 °C. Copper needs only 385 J, so metal heats up fast. That's why oceans and lakes warm and cool slowly, and why towns near big water have milder weather.

The second property is even weirder. Most things get denser when they freeze, but water expands. Ice is about 9% less dense than liquid water, so it floats. Also, water is densest near 4 °C, so the coldest water stays on top in winter and lakes freeze from the top down.

Put those together, and floating ice and slow warming help fish and other life survive the winter. The deep water under the ice stays liquid.

Did you know? Because ice floats so low in the water, about 90% of an iceberg sits below the surface.

6.text:
Glaciers Carved the Great Lakes

Ice is part of the water cycle too, and it reshaped our whole region. A sheet of ice 1 mile thick covered the Great Lakes region and dug out the lake basins.

The ice began to melt back about 20,000 years ago. Meltwater filled the basins, and the lakes reached today's shape about 3,000 years ago. Now the Great Lakes hold about 20% of the world's fresh surface water. In Indiana, the same ice left till and erratics, which you met in Deck 10.

The land is still adjusting. All that ice was so heavy it pushed the ground down. Once-buried land is slowly rising back up, while the land near the old ice edge, which had bulged up, is slowly sinking.

Did you know? The Great Lakes hold about 90% of the fresh surface water in the United States.

7.text:
Venus Lost Its Oceans

How can scientists tell a planet once had water when it's bone dry today? They use the D/H ratio: heavy hydrogen (deuterium) per normal hydrogen. It rises as water escapes. Deuterium is hydrogen with an extra neutron, so it's a bit heavier.

Here's the process. High in the air, UV light splits H2O. Light H escapes to space more easily, while the heavier D stays behind. The more water a planet loses, the more deuterium it has left over.

Compare the D/H ratios with Earth's ocean water, which is set at 1. Mars: about 7. Venus's lower air: about 100. Venus's upper air: about 240. Venus lost a huge amount of water. Today it's 92 bar and 464 °C, and very dry. Because the hydrogen escaped to space, that water can never come back.

Did you know? The two Venus numbers aren't a mistake. They were measured at different heights with different methods, and both show Venus lost lots of water.

8.text:
Present It: Water, Local & Global

Time to show the water cycle in action. You'll make a short presentation with two parts. Part A is a local loop at your school. Where does rain on your school go? Does it run off to a river or a Great Lake? Does it soak in to an aquifer and a well? Include one human effect, like paving, farms or pumping.

Part B is a global loop. Show ocean evaporation and rain on land, and include ice, groundwater and surface water. Show how ocean currents move water (you'll learn more about this in Part 2). Add one global human effect.

Keep it short: one local loop and one global loop, with one human effect each. Cite a source for every number you use.

9.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 1

Think about the water budget on Slide 4. Most of the water that evaporates into the air comes from...

A) lakes and rivers, B) the oceans, C) plants, or D) glaciers? Choose one and explain your reasoning. Remember, the water cycle is global, not just one lake.

10.text:
Tilt Makes the Seasons

Earth's tilt, 23.4°, is the reason for seasons. Not distance! In fact, Earth is closest to the Sun in early January and farthest in early July. If distance mattered most, we'd have summer in January.

Here's what actually happens. The axis keeps pointing the same way as Earth goes around the Sun. In June, the north tips toward the Sun. In December, the north tips away. When your hemisphere tips toward the Sun, sunlight hits more directly, and days are longer.

Why does direct sunlight matter? Picture three rays of light. Direct rays are packed into a small patch, so each spot gets lots of energy. Slanted rays are spread out over a bigger area, so each spot gets less. That's also why the equator is warmer than the poles.

Did you know? Earth's tilt isn't fixed forever. It slowly changes between 22.1° and 24.5°, which you'll see on Slide 24.

11.text:
Mars Has Seasons Too

Mars's tilt is 25.19°, close to Earth's, so it has seasons for the same reason. But Mars's seasons have a twist. Its air is mostly CO2, and in polar winter it gets so cold that CO2 frost (dry ice) forms right out of the air.

That's a lot of air turning to ice. About 25% of Mars's air freezes onto a pole each year (estimates run from 20 to 30%). The cap grows in winter and shrinks in summer, swapping between northern winter and southern winter.

Mars had much more water long ago. Scientists estimate an ancient ocean, 137 m deep if spread out over the whole planet. But 87% of that water was lost to space.

Did you know? Under the seasonal dry ice in the north, there's a permanent cap of regular water ice.

12.text:
Uranus: The Sideways Seasons

If tilt makes seasons, what happens on a planet that's tipped way over? Uranus has a tilt of about 98°, compared with Earth's 23.4°. It's basically rolling around the Sun on its side.

Uranus has an 84-year orbit. That means each pole gets about 42 years of light and then 42 years of dark. One pole gets all-day sun for decades while the other has all-night darkness.

Those are the most extreme seasons of any planet. Near spring and fall, normal-ish days of about 17 hours return.

13.text:
Spin Bends the Winds

If Earth didn't spin, air would rise at the hot equator, flow to the poles, sink and flow back. One simple loop. But Earth does spin, which creates the Coriolis effect: moving air and water curve right in the north and left in the south, as Earth spins.

Because of that curve, each hemisphere gets three circulation cells. The Hadley cell runs from the equator (0°) to 30°, with the trade winds at the surface. The Ferrel cell runs from 30° to 60°, with the westerlies. The Polar cell runs from 60° to 90°N, with the polar easterlies.

Between the cells are pressure bands. There's rising air at L (low pressure) and sinking air at H (high pressure). Lows are at 0° and 60°, and highs are at 30° and 90°N. Rising air brings clouds and rain, while sinking air brings dry, fair weather, which is why many deserts sit near 30°.

Did you know? Indiana sits in the westerlies, so most of our weather rolls in from the west.

14.text:
Wind Drives Surface Currents

Winds push on the ocean's surface and get the water moving. Those currents link up into gyres. A gyre is a large system of rotating ocean currents. There are five major ones, in the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans.

Trade winds push water one way and westerlies push it the other, while the Coriolis effect bends the flow. So gyres spin clockwise in the north and counterclockwise in the south of the equator.

One famous current is the Gulf Stream, on the western edge of the North Atlantic gyre. It carries warm water north, which is why Bergen, Norway, has milder winters than New York, even though it's much farther north.

Did you know? The Gulf Stream carries more water than all the world's rivers combined.

15.text:
The Global Ocean Conveyor

Not all ocean currents are driven by wind. Thermohaline circulation is deep ocean currents driven by density: cold, salty water sinks. "Thermo" means temperature, and "haline" means salt.

Here's how it works. Warm, fresher water floats. When sea ice forms, it leaves salt behind in the water around it. That water becomes cold and salty, so it sinks. It sinks near Norway, after the warm surface flow from the Gulf Stream gives off its heat.

Then the cold deep flow travels south along the bottom of the Atlantic to Antarctica and out into the Indian and Pacific Oceans. There it rises in upwelling and returns as a warm surface flow. It's slow: each m3 of water takes about 1,000 years to finish a loop.

Did you know? Salt doesn't make water float. It makes water denser, so salty water actually sinks.

16.text:
El Niño Shifts the Pacific

Normally, strong trade winds blow from east to west across the tropical Pacific. They pile up a warm pool of water near Asia and Australia and let cold water rise up in cold upwelling near S. America. During La Niña, this normal pattern gets even stronger.

El Niño is the flip side: weak trade winds let warm water spread east across the Pacific. With weak trade winds, the warm pool slides toward S. America, and the storm clouds follow the warm water.

El Niño and La Niña swing back and forth every 3 to 7 years on average. And their effects reach far beyond the Pacific. In a typical El Niño winter, the Gulf Coast tends to be wetter than average, and the Ohio Valley, including Indiana, tends to be drier. Those are tendencies, not guarantees.

Did you know? El Niño isn't a storm. It's an ocean and air pattern that can last for months.

17.text:
Model It: Spin & Sink

Time to build two models. For Model A, the Coriolis model: spin a paper plate counterclockwise and draw a straight line from the center to the edge. Which way did the line curve? Then add the 3 cells and surface winds.

For Model B, the conveyor model: color cold salty water blue and warm water red. Pour each gently into a clear tub and sketch which sinks and which floats. Then draw the conveyor loop on a world map.

Then explain: how could a change in winds or currents cause El Niño?

18.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 2

Put your conveyor model to the test. Why does water sink in the far North Atlantic?

Is it A) wind pushes it down, B) it is cold and salty, so it's dense, C) Coriolis pulls it down, or D) the Moon's tides? Use what you saw in your tub on Slide 17. Choose one and explain.

19.text:
Where Air Masses Meet

An air mass is a huge body of air with about the same temperature and moisture throughout. Two kinds matter a lot for Indiana. Cold, dry air (cP) comes down from Canada. Warm, moist air (mT) comes up from the Gulf of Mexico.

A front is the boundary where two air masses of different density meet. At a cold front, the heavy cold air shoves under the warm air like a snowplow. The warm air is forced up, and that quick lift makes storms along the cold front.

Pressure tells you what's coming. L means rising air and clouds. H means sinking air and fair weather.

Did you know? On weather maps, a cold front is a blue line with triangles, and a warm front is a red line with half circles.

20.text:
Indiana Tornado Country

Indiana averages 22 tornadoes a year, the long-term NWS average. Why here? Warm, moist Gulf air flows north, and when a cold front pushes into it, the air is lifted fast into thunderstorms.

Most tornadoes come from April to June, but every month has had one in Indiana. And 2026 has been wild: 88 by Sept. 10, a record (preliminary). June 2026 alone had 58.

Why do recent averages look higher than older ones? Better radar and more people with cameras mean many more weak tornadoes get reported. That doesn't by itself mean more tornadoes actually happen.

Did you know? Opening windows doesn't save your house in a tornado. The real advice is to stay away from windows.

21.text:
Chart the Weather: 5 Days

Time to be a meteorologist. For five days, record the weather at the same time each day: temperature (°C), pressure (mb), humidity (%), which way the wind is from, clouds, and whether it rained.

Then graph temperature, pressure and humidity on the same time axis. Look for clues of a front passing: falling pressure as a low comes in, then a wind shift, and changes in temperature and humidity.

When the graph is done, circle the day a front passed, and explain each change in writing.

22.text:
Make a Storm Plan

Indiana gets severe weather in both summer and winter, so you need a plan for both. Part A covers summer tornadoes and thunderstorms. First, know the difference: a watch means be ready; a warning means act now. Your safe spot is a basement or interior room, away from windows. If you're in a mobile home, leave it for a sturdier building. And how will you get the warning?

Part B covers winter storms. Build a supply kit for home and car. Plan for losing heat and power. Make sure your CO (carbon monoxide) detector works and the outside vent is clear. And decide who checks on whom.

Write one plan for home and one for school, then practice it.

Did you know? At school, big open rooms like the gym and cafeteria are bad places to shelter from a tornado.

23.text:
Weather Is Not Climate

Weather is what's happening outside hour to hour and day to day. Climate is the average weather of a place over decades, like a 30-year normal. In the U.S., the official climate normal right now is the 1991 to 2020 normal.

On the graph, the thin wiggly line jumps around from Jan to Jul to Dec: that's weather. The smooth line is the climate, the average you'd expect for each time of year.

So one cold week doesn't prove the climate isn't warming. That's weather. Climate is about long-term patterns.

Did you know? A place's climate depends on its latitude, its pressure belt, nearby oceans and currents, and the greenhouse effect.

24.text:
Slow Orbit Cycles Pace Ice Ages

Why has Earth had ice ages? Part of the answer is in Earth's orbit. Milankovitch cycles are slow changes in Earth's orbit, tilt and wobble that shift sunlight.

There are three. Eccentricity is the orbit's shape, stretching and relaxing every about 100,000 years. Obliquity is the tilt, ranging from 22.1° to 24.5° about every 41,000 years. Precession is the wobble of the axis, about every 26,000 years. (The orbit shape is exaggerated and not to scale in the drawing.)

These cycles change how sunlight is spread across the seasons and latitudes, and they line up with ice ages. But they're slow, working over tens of thousands of years. They can't explain the fast warming of the last century.

Did you know? These cycles are caused by the gravity of the Sun, the Moon and the other planets tugging on Earth. The changes in orbit shape come mainly from Jupiter and Venus.

25.text:
CO2 Is Rising Fast

Scientists have measured CO2 at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, since the 1950s. The 2025 annual mean (NOAA GML) was 427 ppm. The graph climbs from about 315 ppm in 1959, past 350 and 400, to 2025.

For comparison, before the 1750s, CO2 was 280 or less. And ice cores show it was never above 300 in 800,000 yrs.

The rise is speeding up, and scientists have concluded that it comes from human activities, mainly burning fossil fuels. The little wiggles in the curve are real, too: they're the seasons, as plants grow in spring and summer and pull CO2 out of the air.

Did you know? People release about 100 times or more CO2 than volcanoes do.

26.text:
Earth Is Warming

2024 was the warmest year on record: +1.28 °C vs the 1951 to 1980 average, according to NASA GISTEMP's yearly data. Compared with 1850 to 1900, before most industry, that's about +1.5 °C.

On the graph, 0 = the 1951 to 1980 average. The line starts below zero, around -0.5 °C, in 1880, and climbs past +0.5 and +1.0 by 2025.

Volcanoes can cause a short dip. Mount Pinatubo erupted in 1991, and its cloud reflected sunlight, cooling the planet by about 0.5 °C. But within about two years, that cooling was gone. A short push isn't a trend.

Did you know? The ten warmest years on record have all come since 2015 (NASA, through 2025).

27.text:
What Climate Models Project

We can't experiment on a spare Earth, so scientists build a climate model: a computer model of air, ocean, ice and land, built from physics, used to project future climate. They test models by checking whether they can reproduce past climate.

Here is the warming by 2081 to 2100, compared with 1850 to 1900 (IPCC). With very low emissions: +1.0 to 1.8 °C. On a middle path: +2.1 to 3.5 °C. With very high emissions: +3.3 to 5.7 °C.

These are projections, not predictions: which future we get depends on what people emit.

28.text:
Rising Seas, More Acidic Ocean

Global sea level has risen 10 cm since 1993, measured by NASA satellites, and the yearly rise is now more than twice as fast as in 1993. By 2100, compared with 1995 to 2014, the IPCC projects +0.28 to 0.55 m if emissions are very low and +0.63 to 1.01 m if very high. Seas rise because warm water expands and melting land ice adds water.

The ocean also absorbs CO2, which makes it more acidic. Ocean pH has dropped about 0.1: that's about 30% more acidic. It could reach about pH 7.8 by 2100 if emissions stay high.

The hazards include coastal flooding, bigger storm surges, and a harder time for corals and shellfish to build their shells.

Did you know? The ocean isn't turning into lemon juice. It's still basic (above pH 7), just less basic than before.

29.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 3

Think about the difference between weather and climate from Slide 23. Which one is about climate, not weather?

Is it A) a tornado hit Indiana yesterday, B) Indiana's 30-year average July high, C) rain is forecast for Friday, or D) this morning's pressure dropped? Pick one and explain. Hint: think about the time span, not how dramatic the event is.

30.text:
Exit Ticket

You followed water, wind and climate around the planet today. Show what you've learned with four questions.

First, Earth is farther from the Sun in July. Why is July still hotter here? Second, how do temperature and salt drive the deep-ocean conveyor? Third, give one sign that climate is changing, with its number and source. Fourth, how can El Niño change Indiana's winter?

When you're done, look back at your "I can" list from Slide 2 and rate yourself again.

31.text:
One More Question

Here's a bonus challenge if you studied the sideways planet on Slide 12.

Uranus is tipped about 98°. Describe one year at its north pole.

32.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards. Here's what they ask you to do, in plain words.

ES.4.3: make a presentation of the water cycle, both local and global, showing how groundwater, surface water and ocean currents connect and how people affect water. ES.4.4: model how the Coriolis effect shapes global winds, and explain how changes in winds and oceans cause El Niño and La Niña. ES.4.5: chart how humidity, pressure and temperature change with the weather, explain winds, clouds and severe storms, and make an emergency plan for summer and winter storms.

ES.4.6: tell weather from climate, explain how Milankovitch cycles (tilt, wobble and orbit shape) pace ice ages, and explain how fast, short-term climate change is different. ES.3.3: explain how events on one side of the world can change weather around the globe, and how natural and human causes affect the air and climate. ES.4.2: model how heat moves through air, land and water, including the deep ocean conveyor.
